Black-billed treehunter nesting biology has been inferred largely from the closely related congener Thripadectes holostictus, given the difficulty of observing this species in its dense Andean cloud forest habitat. Based on those data, the incubation period requires approximately two weeks before hatching, with the estimated age at birth being 15 days [ab = 15 days] when eggs are maintained at an incubation temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. The neonate emerges at a modest wet weight of 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], a value typical of altricial furnariid chicks that depend entirely on parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. This initial body mass is remarkably low relative to the ultimate size the chicks will attain, necessitating a period of rapid growth fueled by frequent arthropod deliveries from both parents. The nestling period proceeds under the sustained brooding efforts of the adults, who must balance the thermal demands of the altricial young against the need to forage extensively in the understory.

Under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active passerine metabolism, typically around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone represents the point at which the young bird achieves sufficient flight feather maturation and neuromuscular coordination to depart the nest, though it remains dependent on parental care for some additional weeks. The relatively short nestling period, extending only three weeks from hatching to fledging, is consistent with the pattern observed in other medium-sized insectivorous passerines inhabiting montane environments where predation risk may favor rapid development. After departing the nest, the fledgling continues to receive food from its parents while learning to forage independently in the bamboo thickets and moss-laden branches that constitute its preferred habitat, gradually acquiring the skills necessary to locate the beetles, caterpillars, and other arthropods that form the bulk of its diet.

Sexual maturity in the Black-billed treehunter is attained relatively quickly for a bird of its body size, with the time since birth at puberty estimated at 63 days [tp = 63 days] when individuals are maintained at a typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This means that young birds are potentially capable of gonadal development and gamete production within just over two months of hatching, a relatively rapid maturation rate among the Furnariidae. However, despite the early physiological capacity for reproduction, actual breeding is typically deferred until the following year, likely due to the constraints of territory acquisition, pair formation, and the need to develop proficient foraging skills in a complex three-dimensional habitat. The rapid pubertal development may serve as an adaptive hedge, allowing individuals that encounter favorable conditions or vacant territories to capitalize on breeding opportunities earlier than would otherwise be possible. This developmental trajectory is consistent with the life history strategies of many tropical insectivorous passerines.

First brood initiation occurs substantially later than the attainment of puberty, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at approximately 511 days [tR = approximately 511 days] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay of over a year between hatching and first successful reproduction reflects the significant challenges faced by young birds in establishing a breeding territory within the saturated montane forest environment. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as females producing approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], each containing 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], yields a modest annual output that is characteristic of many tropical passerines investing heavily in the survival and quality of each offspring. This reproductive strategy contrasts sharply with temperate-zone congeners, where larger clutch sizes and higher seasonal fecundity are common. The limited reproductive output of Thripadectes melanorhynchus appears tied to the constraints of prolonged parental care and the challenging nature of foraging in dense understory vegetation.

Longevity records for the Black-billed treehunter indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3,358 days [am = approximately 3,358 days] under the standard physiological temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], an exceptional duration among small-bodied insectivorous passerines that reflects the slow-life-history pace typical of tropical montane avifauna. Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained through respirometry trials yield an oxygen consumption of 98.18 milliliters per hour [JOi = 98.18 milliliters per hour] at the same body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value consistent with the energetic demands of a 44.3 grams [Wwi = 44.3 grams] adult female maintaining endothermy in cool cloud forest conditions. This adult body mass situates Thripadectes melanorhynchus among the larger members of its genus, requiring substantial daily food intake to meet its metabolic requirements amidst the challenges of a high-elevation environment.
